content: The global prevalence of unplanned pregnancies and abortions among young women highlights the urgent need for improved access to modern contraceptive services. In sub-Saharan Africa, the birth rate among females aged 15 to 19 years is 121 per 1000, while in the United States, 6% of teenagers in the same age group became pregnant in 2010. Most pregnancies among women up to the age of 25 are unintended. The objective of this study was to identify brief educational interventions that could improve contraceptive use among young people. These interventions needed to be feasible for implementation in resource-limited clinical settings, such as clinics, and were designed to consist of one to three sessions lasting 15 to 60 minutes, with potential follow-up. The primary outcomes assessed were pregnancy rates and contraceptive use. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including CENTRAL, PubMed, POPLINE, Web of Science, ClinicalTrials.gov, and ICTRP, up to March 7, 2016. The inclusion criteria encompassed randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized studies (NRS) involving individuals or clusters of participants aged up to 25 years. Data extraction and analysis were performed by two authors, with methodological quality assessed. For dichotomous outcomes, Mantel-Haenszel odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated, while mean differences (MDs) with 95% CIs were used for continuous variables. Adjusted measures were utilized for cluster RCTs and NRS to account for confounding factors. Due to the heterogeneity of interventions and outcome measures, meta-analysis was not conducted. The review identified 11 studies published between 1983 and 2015, involving a total of 8,338 participants. Ten studies were conducted in the United States, and one in China. Five studies demonstrated some effect on contraceptive use. Among three RCTs that evaluated innovative counseling approaches, one showed a significant intervention effect. Adolescents who received developmental counseling were significantly more likely to use contraception effectively at one year compared to those who received standard counseling (OR 48.38, 95% CI 5.96 to 392.63). Three studies incorporated audiovisual tools alongside counseling, with two reporting positive effects on contraceptive use. One NRS involving young men aged 15 to 18 years used a slide-tape presentation combined with reproductive health consultations. At one year, participants in the intervention group were more likely to report using effective contraception and having a partner who used oral contraceptives during their last sexual encounter (adjusted OR 1.51 and 1.66, respectively). Another study employed a computer-based contraceptive decision-making program alongside standard counseling for women aged up to 20 years. At one site, fewer women in the intervention group had not used oral contraceptives at one year compared to the counseling-only group (3.4% vs. 8.8%; P = 0.05). Three RCTs included phone follow-up after counseling, with one showing a significant effect on contraceptive use among women aged 16 to 24 years. Women who received counseling plus phone calls encouraging contraceptive use were more likely to report consistent oral contraceptive use at three months (OR 1.41, 95% CI 1.06 to 1.87) and six months (OR 1.39, 95% CI 1.03 to 1.87). At three months, they were also more likely to report condom use during their last sexual encounter (OR 1.45, 95% CI 1.03 to 2.03). Two cluster RCTs focused on training healthcare providers in contraceptive methods and counseling. One trial demonstrated an intervention effect by providing comprehensive contraceptive services to women aged up to 25 years post-abortion. At six months, participants in the comprehensive-service group were more likely to use effective contraception (adjusted OR 2.03, 95% CI 1.04 to 3.98) and to use condoms consistently and correctly (adjusted OR 5.68, 95% CI 3.39 to 9.53) compared to the standard-care group. In conclusion, few studies have evaluated brief educational strategies for improving contraceptive use among young people. The studies reviewed exhibited heterogeneity in participants' ages and life circumstances. Of the five studies that demonstrated some effect, one provided moderate-quality evidence, while the remaining four were older studies with low-quality evidence. Although more intensive strategies may yield greater effectiveness, their implementation could pose significant challenges for many clinics.
